newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech IPB owners's group backs managers.
newsitem.headline: Czech IPB owners's group backs managers.

text.p: Leading shareholders of Czech bank IPB a.s. said on Wednesday they did not feel two of the bank's top officials who were charged on Tuesday with fraud had damaged shareholder interests.
Investigators said on Tuesday that two senior IPB officials had been charged with fraud but declined to name them.
However, IPB supervisory board member Jan Suchanek confirmed to Reuters the two men charged were Director Jiri Tesar and his deputy Libor Prochazka.

The shareholders group, which collectively holds about half of IPB's stock, issued a statement saying it trusted actions taken by the two in connection with a police investigation into the bank's dealings.
"The undersigned shareholders are not of the opinion that they were damaged in the case by Mr. Tesar and Mr. Prochazka," the statement said.

The signatories included Charouz Holding a.s., which holds 11.9 percent, Bankovni Holding a.s. (10.7 percent), Nutshell s.r.o. (9.8 percent), Vojenske Stavby a.s. (9.0 percent), state-held Ceska Posta a.s. (4.5 percent), P.I.F. a.s. (3.0 percent) and V-Invest Holding which has an unknown stake.
Bankovni Holding is controlled by IPB.

"The undersigned shareholders...are expressing serious concerns over the consequences and damages which the charge can have for all shareholders of IPB and the Czech banking sector as a whole," the statement said.
Shareholders would assess any damages caused by the investigation at an extraordinary general meeting, it said.

Suchanek, who said he represented private shareholders, said he had not seen the shareholders' statement but agreed that the case was "totally unjustified" and "interfered" with the rights of a private subject.
"The trade (being investigated) very significantly increased the value of the bank's assets," he said.
Local media have reported that the case under investigation involved IPB's 180 million crown purchase of real estate in Prague, but investigators declined to comment on the matter.

IPB is the third largest Czech bank by basic capital. The government privatisation agency National Property Fund (NPF) holds a 31.5 percent stake in IPB bringing the state's total holding to 36 perecnt together with Ceska Posta.

The NPF said on Tuesday evening that if it did not get a "satisfactory explanation" from IPB, or if the bank had not taken "sufficient measures" by next Tuesday, it would call an extraordinary general meeting of IPB to resolve personnel questions.

The state holdings should be sold off in the middle of the year and local press reports say ING Bank and Japan's Nomura are frontrunners on the shortlist of buyers, being drawn up by U.S based investment bank Salomon Brothers.
The NPF said on Tuesday after the charges were published that the case should not affect the privatisation process.
IPB's shares dropped 16 crowns in active trading on Wednesday to close at 304 crowns as the market was mulling the charges.
